title: Home and housing
objectives: I can explain why armário, prédio, sofá, aluguel and the other words of the home are written and pronounced as they are.
I can say what there is in a place with tem, and explain why it never changes for singular or plural.
I can say where something is with ficar and estar, and join the preposition to the article (ao lado do, em frente à).
I can describe a home with agreeing adjectives, and choose the right form of muito, pouco, bastante and tanto.
I can ask about an apartment to rent, including the rent, the floor and the condomínio.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: a single s between two vowels is [z], so casa is said KA-za, and the final unstressed a is weak. Em casa, with no article, means at home.

example.target: A minha casa é pequena, mas é clara.
example.source: My house is small, but it is bright.
example.source_literal: The my house is small, but is bright.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: a-par-ta-MEN-to. It ends in o, so the stress falls on the second to last syllable by default and no accent is needed. The en before t is a nasal vowel, because the n ends its syllable. The casual short form is apê, a-PÊ: it ends in e but is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs an accent, and the closed e takes the circumflex.

example.target: Eu moro em um apartamento no centro.
example.source: I live in an apartment downtown.
example.source_literal: I live in an apartment in-the center.

vocabulary.note: Sala is any large room or hall. In a home it is the living room, so a sala is the room where people sit together. Spelling: s at the start of a word is [s].

example.source: The sofa is in the living room.

vocabulary.note: Also a room in the sense of a place to sleep, such as a hotel room. The same word means fourth and quarter. Spelling and sound: qua is [kwa], with the u said like the English w of 'quick', and the r ends the first syllable, so its sound depends on the region.

Spelling and sound: co-ZI-nha. The z is [z]. The pair nh is one sound [ɲ], like the ny of canyon, and the vowel before it takes a light nasal colour. Ends in a, so the stress is on the second to last syllable.

Built from banho (bath) plus the suffix -eiro. A suffix is an ending added to a word to build a new word, and -eiro names a person or place connected with the original word. Spelling and sound: ba-NHEI-ro. The nh is [ɲ], and ei is a diphthong said like English 'ay' in day. Ends in o, so the stress is on the second to last syllable, the diphthong, and no accent is needed.

Spelling and sound: va-RAN-da. The n ends its syllable, so the a before it is nasal [ɐ̃], and nd is split between syllables. The r between vowels is a single quick tap of the tongue, like the tt of American English 'butter'. Ends in a, so the stress is on the second to last syllable.

Spelling and sound: quin-TAL [kĩˈtaw]. Before i, qu is [k] and the u is silent. The in is nasal. The final l is said [w], like the end of English 'now'. A word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default, so it needs no accent. Plural: quintais.

example.target: O quintal fica atrás da casa.
example.source: The backyard is behind the house.
example.source_literal: The backyard stays behind of-the house.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: ga-RA-gem [gaˈɾaʒẽj̃]. The first g is hard because a follows it, and the second g is soft [ʒ] because e follows it. A final em is a nasal diphthong, said like 'ayn' through the nose, and em predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent is needed.

Spelling and sound: so-FÁ. A word ending in a is stressed on the second to last syllable by default, and sofá is stressed on the last, so it needs an accent. The vowel is open, so the accent is the acute. Plural: sofás.

example.target: Tem um sofá azul na sala.
example.source: There is a blue sofa in the living room.
example.source_literal: Has a sofa blue in-the room.

vocabulary.note: Built from gelado (chilled, frozen) plus the suffix -eira, which names a thing that does or holds something. Spelling and sound: ge-la-DEI-ra. The g before e is soft [ʒ], and ei is the diphthong of day. Ends in a, so the stress is on the second to last syllable.

example.source: The refrigerator is in the kitchen.

vocabulary.note: Built from fogo (fire) plus the suffix -ão, which often makes a word bigger. Spelling and sound: fo-GÃO. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone marks both the nasal sound and the stress. The g before a and o is hard. Plural: fogões.

Spelling and sound: ar-MÁ-ri-o. The stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so an accent is always written. The vowel is open, so it is the acute. Compare padaria, where the stress is on the second to last syllable and no accent is needed.

example.target: Tem um armário grande no quarto.
example.source: There is a big closet in the bedroom.
example.source_literal: Has a closet big in-the bedroom.

vocabulary.note: Any building, and in speech usually an apartment building. Spelling and sound: PRÉ-di-o. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so an accent is always written, and the open e takes the acute. The d before the sound i is said [dʒ], like the j of jeans.

example.target: O meu prédio tem oito andares.
example.source_literal: The my building has eight floors.

vocabulary.note: The same word as the verb andar, to walk. The ground floor is o térreo, TÉR-re-o, which is stressed on the third to last syllable and so has an accent, and its rr is one strong r. The first floor above the ground is o primeiro andar. Floors use ordinal numbers: primeiro, segundo, terceiro, quarto, quinto (fifth), so no quinto andar is on the fifth floor. Spelling and sound: an-DAR. The an is nasal, and a word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default. Plural: andares.

example.source: I live on the fifth floor.

vocabulary.note: Built from elevar (to raise) plus the suffix -dor, which names the thing or person that does an action. Spelling and sound: e-le-va-DOR. A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is needed.

example.source: The building does not have an elevator.

vocabulary.note: Also the name of the apartment complex or building association itself. It comes from con- (together) and domínio (ownership). Spelling and sound: con-do-MÍ-ni-o. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so an accent is always written. The letter i has only one quality, so the acute accent only marks the stress. The on is nasal.

example.source: The condominium fee costs three hundred reais.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: a-lu-GUEL [aluˈgɛw]. Before e, gu is a hard [g] and the u is silent. The final l is said [w]. A word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is needed. The plural is aluguéis, and there the accent appears, because the stressed diphthong éi is open, as in papel and papéis.

example.target: O aluguel é mil e quinhentos reais.
example.source: The rent is one thousand five hundred reais.
example.source_literal: The rent is thousand and five-hundred reais.

vocabulary.note: It means both to rent from someone and to rent out to someone, and the context decides. Spelling and sound: a-lu-GAR. The g before a is hard, and the infinitive ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable without an accent. It is a regular -ar verb.

example.source: I want to rent an apartment.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a vizinha. Spelling and sound: vi-ZI-nho. The z is [z], and nh is [ɲ], like the ny of canyon. Ends in o, so the stress is on the second to last syllable.

example.target: O meu vizinho é muito barulhento.
example.source_literal: The my neighbor is very noisy.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: BAI-rro. The ai is a diphthong said like English 'eye'. The rr between vowels is one strong r sound, and it is not split in pronunciation.

Spelling and sound: GRAN-de [ˈgɾɐ̃dʒi]. The g stays hard before r. The an is nasal. The final e is said i, so the d before it is [dʒ], like the j of jeans. Ends in e, so the stress is on the second to last syllable. It has one form for masculine and feminine: grande, grandes.
Spelling and sound: pe-QUE-no. Before e, qu is [k] and the u is silent. Ends in o, so the stress is on the second to last syllable. Feminine: pequena.

Claro means clear, and a room full of light is a clear room. Said on its own, Claro! means of course. Spelling and sound: CLA-ro. The c before l is [k], and the r between vowels is a single quick tap of the tongue, like the tt of American English 'butter'. Feminine: clara.

Built from barulho (noise) plus the suffix -ento, which means full of. Spelling and sound: ba-ru-LHEN-to. The pair lh is one sound [ʎ], like the lli of million, and the en is nasal. Ends in o, so the stress is on the second to last syllable. Feminine: barulhenta.

Spelling and sound: tran-QUI-lo [tɾɐ̃ˈkwilu]. This is one of the few words where the u after q is pronounced even before i. Until 2009 a trema marked it, and since then you learn the word. Feminine: tranquila.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of the home
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this lesson can be read and written with the rules from the first three lessons, and this note shows how. The method is the same each time. Count the syllables and find the stressed one. Read the default from the ending: a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a plural s), am, em or ens is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else, such as i, u, l, r, z or ão, is stressed on the last. A written accent appears only when the word breaks that default. So an accent is never decoration. It is information about where the stress falls or how open the vowel is.

The first pattern is the proparoxytone, a word stressed on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts that stress, so such a word always carries an accent: armário (ar-MÁ-ri-o), prédio (PRÉ-di-o), condomínio (con-do-MÍ-ni-o), térreo (TÉR-re-o), ótimo (Ó-ti-mo). A final io or eo counts as two syllables in this analysis, so the stressed vowel is third from the end, even though in fast speech the last two vowels often blur into one beat. The mark follows the vowel quality: an open a, e or o takes the acute (a closed e or o would take the circumflex), and i has only one quality, so its acute only marks the stress. Compare padaria (pa-da-RI-a). Its stressed vowel is the i itself, second from the end, which is exactly what the ending a predicts, so it needs no accent, just like tia. What decides the accent is where the stress falls, not the letters ia or io.

The second pattern is nasality. A vowel followed by m or n that ends its syllable is nasal, and the m or n only signals that: apartamento, varanda, quintal, grande, bastante, condomínio. The tilde marks the nasal sound on a and o, and when no other accent is present it also marks the stress: fogão, tão. A word-final em is a nasal diphthong, said like 'ayn' through the nose: tem, garagem. The third pattern is consonant spelling. The letter after a c or g chooses its sound: g is hard in garagem (before a) and soft [ʒ] in geladeira and the end of garagem (before e). Qu and gu keep the hard sound before e and i, with a silent u: pequeno, aluguel, esquina, quinto. Before a, qu is [kw]: quarto, quatro. Tranquilo is one of the few words where the u is pronounced before i. The pairs nh, lh and rr are single sounds: cozinha, vizinho, barulhento, bairro. A final l is said [w]: quintal, aluguel. In most of Brazil the sound i, whether written i or as a final unstressed e, makes a d or t before it say [dʒ] or [tʃ]: grande, bastante, prédio, ótimo.

Several words here are built from a shorter word plus a suffix, an ending added to a word to make a new word with a related meaning. Knowing the suffix tells you the meaning and the stress at once, because the stress sits where the ending puts it: banho (bath) with -eiro gives banheiro, a place for the bath; gelado (chilled) with -eira gives geladeira, a thing that keeps food chilled; fogo (fire) with -ão gives fogão, literally a big fire; barulho (noise) with -ento gives barulhento, full of noise; elevar (to raise) with -dor gives elevador, a thing that raises. English does the same with -er, -ness and -ful. Spelling can shift at the join, as banho becomes banh- before -eiro.

Two plural facts follow from this. The ending l becomes is: quintal, quintais; real, reais. In reais and animais the ai is not open, so no accent is needed. In aluguéis, as in papel and papéis, the stressed éi is open, and so the acute appears. The word ônibus does not change in the plural, because it ends in an unstressed s.

A few other words in this lesson follow plain rules. Luz ends in z, so the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is needed, and final z is [s] or [ʃ] by region. Espaço has a ç, which writes [s] before o. Escuro has an s that ends its syllable, so it is [s] or [ʃ] by region, and a c before u that is [k]. Barulho and velho have lh. Há (there is, in the formal form) is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, so it carries an acute, and the accent also keeps it apart from a (the article or the preposition to), which has no stress of its own. Atrás and lá follow the same logic: the stress is on the last syllable although the ending predicts the second to last. The next note shows tem and têm.

rows: Ends in a, which predicts the second to last syllable. The stress is last, so an acute is written. The a is open.
No ending predicts third to last stress, so an accent is always written. Open a, so the acute.
Same rule. Open e takes the acute. The d before the sound i is [dʒ].
Same rule. The acute on i only marks the stress. The on is nasal.
The stressed i is second to last, as the ending a predicts. No accent.
Ending ão predicts the last syllable. The tilde marks the nasal sound and the stress.
Ending l predicts the last syllable. The u after g is silent. Final l is [w]. Plural aluguéis.
The u after q is silent. The in is nasal. Final l is [w].
The qua is [kwa]. The r ends the syllable, so its sound depends on the region.
The u is pronounced here: [kwi]. Since 2009 no trema marks it.
Before e, qu is [k] and the u is silent.
The z is [z]. The nh is one sound [ɲ], like the ny of canyon.
The lh is one sound [ʎ], like the lli of million. The en is nasal.
First g is hard before a. Second g is soft [ʒ] before e. Final em is a nasal diphthong.
The an is nasal. The g is hard before r. The final e is said i, so the d is [dʒ].
Third to last stress, so an accent. Open o takes the acute. The t before i is [tʃ].
A stressed one-syllable word ending in a takes an accent. It also separates há from a.

grammar.title: Tem and há: saying what exists
grammar.explanation:
English says there is or there are, and the verb changes with the noun that follows: there is a sofa, there are two bedrooms. The word there is a dummy subject, a placeholder that fills the subject position because an English sentence needs one. Portuguese needs no placeholder, because the verb of existence has no subject at all. A verb with no subject has nothing to agree with, so it stays in the third person singular, the form used for he, she, it and você. In everyday Brazilian speech that verb is tem, from ter, which also means to have. In careful writing and formal speech it is há, from haver, an older verb that in daily use survives mostly in this meaning. Neither form ever turns plural: tem dois quartos, tem muitas janelas, há dois quartos.

The same ter also means to have or to contain when it has a subject: o apartamento tem dois quartos says that the apartment has two bedrooms. Brazilians do not feel a boundary between the two ideas, because a place that has two bedrooms is a place where two bedrooms exist. The difference is only grammatical. When a person is the subject, ter is conjugated normally: eu tenho, você tem, nós temos, eles têm. The plural têm carries a circumflex, a differential accent (see the lesson on accents): têm and tem sound the same, and the accent only shows the plural in writing. The existential tem never takes it, because the existential verb is never plural. Há has an acute accent for the reason given in the spelling note: it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a.

Questions and negatives follow the usual Portuguese rules, with no helper verb like English do. A question is the statement said with rising intonation, tem varanda?, and a negative puts não before the verb, não tem elevador. A short answer repeats the verb: tem varanda? Tem, sim. The word sim only adds emphasis. The place can come at the start or the end: tem um banco aqui, or aqui tem um banco. Portuguese often leaves out the article when asking whether a kind of thing exists: tem garagem? means is there a garage?, with garage as a category. Use um or uma when you point to one item being counted: tem uma mesa e quatro cadeiras.

grammar.title: Muito, pouco, bastante and tanto: quantity words
grammar.explanation:
A quantity word says how much or how many. English splits the job: many goes with things you can count, much with things you cannot, and very goes with adjectives (many windows, much noise, very big). Portuguese has one family of words, muito, pouco, bastante and tanto, and it chooses the form by looking at the word that follows. This works because Portuguese keeps two kinds of words apart. Before a noun, the quantity word acts as an adjective, and an adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number, like any other adjective (see the lesson on gender, number and agreement). Before an adjective or another adverb, or after a verb, it acts as an adverb, a word that modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb, and an adverb has no gender or number, so it never changes.

So muito barulho, muita luz, muitos quartos and muitas janelas match their nouns. But a casa é muito grande keeps muito because it modifies the adjective grande, not casa, so muita grande is wrong. Eu gosto muito do bairro keeps muito because it modifies a verb. The test is to ask what the word is attached to. Pouco follows the same rule and means little or few: pouco espaço, poucas janelas, pouco claro. Pouco carries the idea that it is not enough, and um pouco de means a little, some. English draws the same line: little light, a shortage, versus a little light, some. Tem pouca luz complains about the light, and tem um pouco de luz states that there is some. In the same way, o bairro é pouco barulhento means not very noisy, and o bairro é um pouco barulhento means a little noisy.

Bastante comes from bastar, to be enough, so its core idea is enough or plenty: bastante espaço. Before an adjective it means quite or fairly, a little weaker than muito: bastante tranquilo. Before a plural noun careful writing uses bastantes (bastantes janelas), and speech often leaves bastante unchanged. Tanto means so much or so many and agrees before a noun: tanto barulho, tanta gente, tantos quartos. Gente is a feminine singular noun, so you say tanta gente and muita gente even though it means people. Before an adjective, tanto shortens to tão, with a tilde, because the ending ão is stressed and the tilde marks both the nasal sound and the stress: tão grande, tão barulhenta. In speech, bem is also used to strengthen an adjective: a sala é bem grande means the living room is really big. The question word quanto belongs to the same family and agrees the same way before a noun: quantos quartos tem?, quanta luz tem? Standing alone in quanto é? it does not change.

rows: muito espaço, muita luz, muitos quartos, muitas janelas
pouco espaço, pouca luz, poucos quartos, poucas janelas

grammar.title: Estar and ficar for location
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese splits the English verb to be into several verbs, each with its own job. Ser says what something is, estar says how or where it is at the moment, and ficar, whose basic meaning is to stay or to remain, says where something is located. The logic of ficar is that a fixed thing stays where it is. A cozinha fica ao lado da sala literally says that the kitchen stays next to the living room. So ficar suits things that do not move, such as rooms, buildings, streets and cities. Estar is the verb for things that can move and for the position of a person: o Pedro está em casa, as chaves estão em cima da mesa. For furniture, which can be moved but usually is not, speakers use either verb: o sofá está na sala and o sofá fica na sala are both normal.

To ask where something is, use onde fica...? for a place and onde está...? for a person or a movable thing. You will also hear onde é...? for places, but ficar is always safe. The word que before a noun asks which or what: em que andar fica o apartamento? is on which floor is the apartment? The same word begins an exclamation, and the question mark or exclamation mark and the intonation tell them apart.

To be precise about position, Portuguese uses a preposition phrase, a short group of words that ends in the preposition de or a. A preposition joins to the article that follows it, as the contractions lesson explains: ao lado de + o fogão = ao lado do fogão, dentro de + o armário = dentro do armário, embaixo de + a cama = embaixo da cama. Em frente a ends in the preposition a, so it fuses with a feminine article into à, the crase, and with a masculine article into ao: em frente à janela, em frente ao prédio. To test it, replace the feminine word by a masculine one. If you would say ao, the feminine word takes à. Entre does not contract: entre a cama e a janela. Many of these phrases are built from a preposition plus a noun, so em cima de is literally in top of and ao lado de is literally to the side of.

grammar.title: Describing places
grammar.explanation:
A description joins a noun to an adjective, and it needs two decisions: which verb of being, and which form of the adjective. For the verb, ser states what a thing is like as a lasting characteristic, and estar states a condition at the moment of speaking (see the lesson on ser and estar). A casa é grande is a fact about the house. Hoje a rua está barulhenta says that the street is noisy today, as opposed to its usual state. English uses is for both and leaves the difference unmarked.

The adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number. Adjectives ending in o have four forms, claro, clara, claros, claras. Adjectives ending in e or l have one form for both genders. Those in e add s in the plural (grande, grandes), and those in l change l to is (azul, azuis). Adjectives usually follow the noun, the reverse of English: uma sala grande, a big living room. Exclamations use que followed by a noun or an adjective, usually with no verb and no article: Que apartamento claro! is What a bright apartment!, and the English a is simply not translated. Que legal! is How nice! Legal also means lawful, and in everyday speech it means cool or nice. Only the exclamation mark at the end signals the exclamation, because Portuguese has no inverted mark at the start.

To join two descriptions use e (and) or mas (but): a casa é pequena, mas é muito clara. Do not confuse mas with mais, more. In mais the diphthong ai is the signal, so the two are pronounced differently. Use muito, pouco, bastante or bem before the adjective to adjust it, as the previous note explains: muito claro, bastante tranquilo, pouco barulhento.

culture.title: Casas, apartamentos and condomínios
culture.text:
Most people in large Brazilian cities live in an apartamento in a prédio, often with a porteiro who controls the entrance all day. People in smaller towns and suburbs more often live in a casa with a quintal. Many apartments have a small varanda with a churrasqueira, a grill for the weekend barbecue, and most homes have an área de serviço, a small space next to the kitchen with the washing machine.

When you rent, you usually pay two amounts each month: the aluguel to the owner and the condomínio to the building, which covers shared costs such as the porteiro, cleaning and the elevator. There may also be an annual property tax called IPTU. Renting usually requires a fiador, a guarantor, or a security deposit. The person who manages the building is the síndico, and residents meet in an assembleia.

A kitchenette apartment is called a quitinete, and a very small apartment is often called an apê in casual speech. Floors are counted from the térreo, the ground floor, so the primeiro andar is the first floor above it. In many buildings the elevator buttons show T for térreo and sometimes G for garagem.

The words in this note follow the rules of the first lessons. Síndico (SÍN-di-co) and térreo (TÉR-re-o) are stressed on the third to last syllable, so they carry an accent. Churrasqueira has ch [ʃ], a strong rr and a silent u after q. Quitinete also has a silent u after q. Assembleia has no accent, because the 2009 spelling agreement removed the acute from the open diphthong ei in words stressed on the second to last syllable.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese with the English
Which sentence says 'There are two bedrooms'?
choices: Têm dois quartos.
Tem dois quartos.
Temos dois quartos.
São dois quartos.
exercises.explanation: The verb of existence has no subject, so it stays in the third person singular: tem, with no accent. Têm is the plural of ter with a plural subject.

exercises.audio_target: Tem dois quartos e uma varanda.
choices: It has three bedrooms and a yard.
It has two bedrooms and a balcony.
It has two bathrooms and a garage.

exercises.hint_source: There is no elevator in the building.
exercises.explanation: Existence takes tem or há with no subject, and não goes before the verb.

exercises.prompt: In 'Tem muitos quartos na casa' the verb stays tem even though quartos is plural. Why?
choices: Quartos is masculine, and masculine nouns take tem
Muitos already shows the plural, so the verb does not need to
The verb has no subject, so nothing makes it agree with the noun that follows
Têm is used only in writing
exercises.explanation: In English the dummy subject there is followed by is or are. Portuguese has no subject here, so the verb has nothing to agree with.

exercises.prompt: Why does armário carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts
It ends in o, so the default stress is on the last syllable
The accent shows that the a is nasal
The accent separates it from another word, armario
exercises.explanation: No ending predicts stress on the third to last syllable, so such a word always carries an accent. The a is open, so the accent is the acute.

exercises.prompt: Padaria is stressed on the ri, yet it has no accent. Why?
choices: Words that end in ia never take an accent
The ri is a glide, so the word has three syllables
Padaria is a loan word, and loan words take no accent
The stressed ri is the second to last syllable, which is the default for a word ending in a
exercises.explanation: An accent appears only when the stress breaks the default of the ending. Compare família, where the stress is third from the end.

exercises.prompt: How is the final l of quintal pronounced in Brazilian Portuguese?
choices: Like the English l in 'light'
Like the w at the end of English 'now', so the last syllable rhymes with 'now'
It is silent
Like the Portuguese strong r
exercises.explanation: An l that ends a syllable is said [w]. Brasil, sal and aluguel work the same way.

exercises.hint_source: There are many windows in the living room.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, muito is an adjective and agrees with it: janelas is feminine and plural, so muitas.

choices: A casa é muito grande.
A casa é muita grande.
A casa é muitos grande.
exercises.explanation: Before an adjective, muito is an adverb. It modifies grande, not casa, and an adverb never changes.

exercises.hint_source: The bedroom is not very bright.
exercises.explanation: Pouco before an adjective is an adverb meaning not very. It does not agree with quarto or with claro.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'tem pouca luz' and 'tem um pouco de luz'?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
Pouca luz means a lot of light, and um pouco de luz means none
Pouca luz means not much light, which is a shortage, and um pouco de luz means a little light, which is some
Pouca luz is formal and um pouco de luz is informal
exercises.explanation: English draws the same line: little light means not enough, and a little light means some.

exercises.audio_target: O aluguel é mil e quinhentos reais.
choices: The rent is 1,500 reais.
The rent is 1,050 reais.
The rent is 500 reais.

exercises.hint_source: There is so much noise in the street!
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, tanto agrees with it: barulho is masculine singular.
Before an adjective, tanto shortens to tão, which never changes.

choices: The apartment has a lot of light.
The apartment has no windows.
The apartment has little light.

exercises.prompt: Why is ficar a natural verb for 'where the kitchen is'?
choices: Its basic meaning is to become, and a kitchen becomes part of the house
It is a formal verb used only in writing
It means to be tired, which describes a place
Its basic meaning is to stay or remain, and a fixed place stays where it is
exercises.explanation: A cozinha fica ao lado da sala is literally the kitchen stays next to the living room.
Pedro is a person who can move, so the verb is estar. Ficar is for fixed places such as buildings and rooms.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'em frente à janela' and not 'em frente a janela'?
choices: The grave accent shows that janela is stressed on the last syllable
Janela is plural, and the accent marks the plural
Em frente a ends in the preposition a, which fuses with the feminine article a into à
The accent opens the vowel, as in sofá
exercises.explanation: The grave accent has one job, crase, which records the fusion of two a sounds. Before a masculine word the same phrase gives ao: em frente ao prédio.

exercises.prompt_target: A cadeira está em frente ___ janela.
exercises.hint_source: The chair is in front of the window.
exercises.explanation: Em frente a plus the feminine article a gives à. Test: before a masculine word you would say ao.

exercises.prompt_target: O banheiro fica ao lado ___ cozinha.
exercises.hint_source: The bathroom is next to the kitchen.
exercises.explanation: Ao lado de ends in the preposition de, which contracts with the article a: de plus a gives da.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of aluguel?
choices: aluguels
aluguéis
alugueis
alugueles
exercises.explanation: The ending l becomes is, and the stressed éi is open, so the acute accent appears, as in papel and papéis.

exercises.prompt_target: A varanda é pequena, ___ é bonita.
exercises.hint_source: The balcony is small, but it is pretty.
exercises.explanation: Mas means but. Mais means more and is said with the diphthong ai.

exercises.prompt: In 'Que apartamento claro!' what does que do?
choices: It begins an exclamation, with a noun and an adjective and no article, meaning 'What a bright apartment!'
It asks a question, 'Which apartment is bright?'
It means that, and it joins two clauses
It means because
exercises.explanation: Que before a noun or adjective in an exclamation means what or how, and Portuguese does not translate the English a.

exercises.prompt_source: There is a sofa in the living room.
The kitchen is next to the living room.
The sofa is in front of the window.
Does the building have an elevator?
There is no elevator in the building.
The living room has little light.
The refrigerator is in the kitchen.
Does the apartment have a balcony?

exercises.prompt: Why is garagem pronounced with two different g sounds, as in ga-RA-gem?
choices: The first g is hard because a follows it, and the second is soft [ʒ] because e follows it
Both g letters are hard, and the m changes the second
The second g is silent
The first g is soft because it begins the word
exercises.explanation: The vowel after g decides its sound: a, o and u give the hard sound, e and i give the soft one.
Aluguéis is plural, so the verb of being takes a plural form: são for the rents as a general fact, estão for how they are at the moment. Tem and há have no subject, but this sentence has one.

exercises.prompt: Hoje a rua está barulhenta. Why estar and not ser?
choices: Rua is feminine, and feminine nouns take estar
It describes a condition of the street today, not its usual character
Estar is the only verb used with adjectives ending in a
Ser cannot be used with barulhenta
exercises.explanation: Estar presents a condition at the moment of speaking. A rua é barulhenta would describe the street as noisy by nature.

exercises.prompt: Banheiro is built from banho plus -eiro. What does a suffix do?
choices: It is an ending added to a word to build a new, related word
It marks the plural
It marks the stressed syllable with an accent
It is a preposition joined to an article
exercises.explanation: Banho (bath) plus -eiro gives banheiro, a place for the bath, as geladeira comes from gelar plus -eira.

pairs.source: accent: ends in a, stressed last
tilde alone: nasal sound and stress
no accent: ends in l, stressed last
no accent: final a, second to last
